vignette: Elias sits across from me, his hands resting flat on the chair arms, knuckles pale. Over fourteen months, I have learned to listen to what he leaves out as much as what he voices. At fifty-six, his posture still carries the rigid alignment of a man who spent three decades reading instruments in three hundred-mile-per-hour cockpits. He traces the edge of a wooden box his grandfather carved in Bavaria, a quiet habit he has developed as the months have stretched into years. When he speaks, his voice is steady but measured, as if each syllable must be weighed before release. He talks about the rain against the clinic window, then stops, his gaze fixing on the drop of water sliding down the glass. The accident happened on a clear Tuesday in November. He was flying a low-visibility training sortie, running procedures he had executed thousands of times. A hydraulic line failed without warning. The control surfaces went dead. He remembers the sudden, absolute silence of a machine that had never been silent before, then the violent shudder as the airframe buckled. He pulled the ejection handle. The canopy blew, the seat fired, and the G-force dragged him into a sky that suddenly felt too large, too empty. He landed hard in a pine forest, cracked ribs puncturing lung tissue, but walked away. The physical scars faded. The ground did not. In the months that followed, his body healed, but his mind refused to follow. He finds himself standing at the edge of taxiways at the old airbase, watching training flights kick up dust, his breath catching in his throat as he waits for a sound that never comes. When a passenger jet flies overhead, his hands instinctively reach for a throttle that isn't there. He stops sleeping. The bedroom feels like a drop zone. He arranges his pillows against the wall, checks the deadbolt four times, and lies awake tracking the hum of the refrigerator, counting seconds until his heart slows. His wife, Clara, leaves a glass of water on the nightstand every morning. He never touches it. He tries to maintain routine. He waters his garden, tends to the roof, and sits with his grandchildren at the kitchen table. But his attention fractures. When his grandson drops a metal pan, Elias flinches so sharply his knee hits the cabinet. He smiles, makes a joke about getting old, but his jaw stays locked for hours afterward. He no longer watches airshows. He avoids news segments about aviation accidents, changing the channel before the first second of static. At his post-military logistics job, he double-checks safety protocols until his eyes burn, convincing himself it is diligence rather than dread. When Clara reaches for his hand during dinner, he hesitates, then withdraws it, claiming his fingers are stiff from the cold. He tells himself he is fine. He does not know how to say that the sky no longer belongs to him. We sit in the quiet that follows his words. The rain has stopped. Elias watches the puddles outside, his shoulders gradually dropping, though his fingers continue their slow, circular motion on the chair arm. He speaks about the weight of the years, the quiet loyalty he feels when Clara stays, the strange gratitude that he survived. He does not ask for answers. He simply sits with the memory, letting it settle in the room alongside the ordinary sounds of a Tuesday afternoon.
